utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. We may resume with the present witness. Counsel Puliselic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by: Mr. Puliselic:

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse the interruption, but we do appear to be short of some accused. I see Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic just here, but Mr. Vladimir Santic is not present. You may be concerned to commence proceedings without one of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much for drawing to our attention the absence of one accused. Well, I wonder whether we could ask probably Defence counsel whether they intend to proceed even if in the absence of an accused. No, he's coming. All right. All right. We may now proceed. Thank you, Prosecutor. Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kvasina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We left off at the question where you said that you saw Dragan around the village, that he would greet everyone, that he was always well-disposed, so let me take you further with these questions. Do you know whether Dragan Papic would be outgoing to the people? Would he extend his assistance to them? You mentioned something about wood and the illegal wood cutting, but do you have any additional knowledge in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He helped me too. On one occasion his car -- my car broke down and he came by and fixed it for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask that of him? Did he offer it himself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He just offered to do it himself. He said he knew how to do it and he did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you transport in this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a van in which I bought some carpentry supplies and he -- I was transporting that. He went about fixing it and while I set out to find another vehicle. However, by the time I found the second vehicle he had already fixed the one that had broken down. So he also helped me by driving the second car. And when we arrive at my home he asked -- I asked, "How much do I owe you?" He said, "Nothing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said he fined you when you illegally cut wood?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He fined me, but before that he issued me several warnings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you saw Dragan in a village in a store where you played cards, if I understood you correctly, where you could also have a drink or something?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was a general store in the village, and he would pass by there and he would stop by, he would sit down with the locals, he would play cards or just banter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him in that group in Gornja Veceriska discussing any political issues, that he was sort of forcing certain political views or he was speaking about Muslims on negative terms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. He never discussed politics. For the most part he talked about women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how he dressed? What would he wear when he would go about -- going around the woods?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He would wear a forester's outfit, green outfit, or sometimes in civilian clothes. Sometimes it would be the -- that camouflage uniform jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a camouflage uniform jacket?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was camouflage uniform jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him wearing -- carrying a rifle, and if he did, why do you think he carried a rifle if he did so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did carry a rifle, but it was in wintertime when there was a lot of game around and there were some dangerous wild animals. That's why, I think, he felt he need today carry a gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about these wild animals? What type of game lived there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were bears, and boars and wolves, especially lately there were -- there were -- there was a lot of wolves. I think that it had to do with the wars, when they came down from Slovenia or something after the war had started. So it was dangerous there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall until about what period of time you saw Dragan Papic in the Gornja Veceriska area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw him there until the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Later I saw him after the war ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm only referring to the area of Gornja Veceriska. Did you see him later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, no, no. I only saw him there until the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever come by your house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean before the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He and his wife came, oh, to my place, but I wasn't there, and my mother later told me he was -- that he had come by with his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that you did not -- that you saw him after -- before the war. Did you see something on his face?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: On his face. He had a beard. He was growing a beard. I asked him, "Why are you growing a beard?" He said, "Well, I don't want to shave any more."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does Dragan Papic still have a beard today here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, this is nothing compared to what he used to have. He had a much bigger beard before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. He had a bigger beard then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked to him did Dragan ever say -- tell something about himself, about his family, about his wife?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did not speak about himself. He was just talking about how he would like that his wife gave birth to a son, because she was pregnant at the time. I cannot recall anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he said that he would like to have a son?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about him having any conflicts with anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever notice that he was violent or have you heard about him ever being violent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I never heard that, and I never noticed him being violent when we were in the company of other people. From what I could notice, I could not notice anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in closing, what could you say about Papic, about his character, about his personality? If you were to sum it up in just a couple of comments, could you say that he was -- he had a positive character?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could say that he associated with people, he helped people as much as he could. He did not distinguish between different people. He was sociable. He didn't mistreat anyone, he always was the first to greet people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You started to say something and I may have interrupted you. You said that you saw him after the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in Vitez. I asked him, "Where do you work now?" He said, "I work in Impregnacija as a guard."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he no longer worked in Sumarija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He couldn't have been because the forest had disappeared. That is, the forests which he had guarded were now under Muslim control. There were -- the defence line was close by and the area was mined. You couldn't pass through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in other words, he said that he -- he said that he worked with another company. Do you remember anything else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall now. Maybe we talked about something else but now I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my questioning of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As far as I can see, there will be no further questions by any other colleagues, of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. So the Prosecutor? Before Mr. Blaxill starts with the cross-examination, I wonder whether I could raise an issue. On this particular point, I mean, in this particular case, we -- the Defence counsel is harping on so many minute details which may not be contested by the Prosecution. For instance, what about the beard? Is the Prosecution contesting that the accused had a much longer, bigger beard in 1992/93? If the Prosecutor is not contesting this particular point, I wonder whether it is -- there's any point in repeating -- I mean, going back to this particular issue so many times. We have heard so far about five or six witnesses who have testified about the beard of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, I can certainly confirm certain of these matters. The Prosecution takes no issue with the fact that Mr. Papic was clearly, as my learned colleague, Mr. Terrier, has previously expressed about certain of the traits of the accused, he has -- we have no indications of any bad character in the past; on the contrary. His activities mending motor cars and so forth are fully accepted. The fact that he wore his camouflage coat is not a matter of -- in dispute, and that it was in the context at times with his forestry work, that he carried a rifle as a forestry man, that he indeed had a very full beard at the time. Again, that has been evidenced, I think, in video evidence before Your Honours. So we take no issue with those things, and I think in reality the nature of my own cross-examination will probably indicate that in the main the Prosecution take have little issue with very little that he said about the characters of the accused, as indeed my colleague has previously indicated to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kvasina, good morning to you. My name is Michael Blaxill. I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: As a result of your evidence, I would like to ask you a very few questions, and the first is that is it true to say, isn't it, that the relations between the Croat ethnic group and the Muslim ethnic group in your area was, in fact, very friendly and very normal at least until about the middle of 1992. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They were friendly. Because Muslims would come -- from Donja Veceriska would come to visit Croats in Gornja Veceriska. During the alerts, during the overflights of aeroplanes, they came to Gornja Veceriska because it was in a valley, in a bowl of sorts, so they felt safer up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So in fact if there was any enemy at all in the horizon, you had the common enemy at the time, you felt, of the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, who were performing as you felt -- you know, aggression in the area; is that correct? You can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that period, however, you know, the politics started to set in; and isn't it true that from what political developments went on, the atmosphere began to change between the ethnic Croats and the ethnic Muslims towards the later part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this question a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, we've been told in this Chamber before that in a sense, nobody could help but be affected by the changes that happened between the Muslims and the Croats towards the end of 1992; the atmosphere affected everybody. Would you say that was fair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot tell you specifically -- you mean where I was, in my environment? That was a Croat village. When I went to Vitez, and with whomever I communicated, I behaved normally. At that time I was building a house. So I did not really distinguish between people. Perhaps there were some little confrontations; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were your contacts with Mr. Dragan Papic mainly during -- mainly in your own village area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And of course you've just said that that was in fact a Croat village, so you were all Croats together at that time, in that village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So as regards the relationships of Mr. Papic with Muslim people, is this what you've heard either him say or other people say about him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard from other people and from him, and by people talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm not disputing what you've said about him, sir, because we accept that; it's just your own personal experience, to put in context. You said that he carried the weapon, of course, his weapon, his rifle, because of the wild animals present in the forests around your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he carried the rifle because there was strong -- there were severe winters, and it was a big forest. So in my view, he had to be safe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It may be a small point, Mr. Kvasina, but you mentioned the presence of wolves which you felt had perhaps become worse after the war started. Did you have much of a problem for people in the forest with wolves before the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: What kind of problems are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: A danger to anybody who would be walking in the woods or working in the woods.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was dangerous because there were -- wolves appeared, in addition to the bears which had been there before, so now there were wolves in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So in fact before the war it was still prudent to carry the weapon because of the threat of bears, and after the war started it was worse because of wolves too; thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you say that from your knowledge of Mr. Papic, if he was a man who was placed under threat, or a man who was ordered to serve in the military or something like that, would you say he was also a character who would stand up for himself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never heard that he threatened anyone, that he said anything to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No, I think maybe sir, I didn't express the question for you to understand it properly. I'm saying if it is the other way around, if Mr. Papic was man who felt under threat, do you think he had a strong enough personality that he would stand up for himself if he had to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he was always the same. He was always smiling, he was always joyful. He had a good, cheerful disposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have no further questions Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kvasina, my learned colleague Blaxill asked about the presence of wolves. Would you please say when did the presence of wolves intensify in the area? I believe that you answered my questions -- my question; 'when the war in Croatia started'.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is when their presence intensified in the forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When answering the question by Mr. Blaxill, it appeared as if you said that the presence of wolves intensified after the war started in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no, it was after it started in Slovenia. So people were saying that somehow they drifted down from there, that they were chased out of there. Now they were are around, from where they came I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear up that point. The second question I have is what is -- who lived in Donja Veceriska? You said that in Gornja Veceriska Croats lived, but what about Donja Veceriska, lower Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Both Croats and Muslims lived in Donja Veceriska. About half and half. I don't know exactly the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you know whether Muslims, too, engaged in illegal woodcutting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims did as well as the Serbs, in addition to the Croat villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Did the Muslims from Donja Veceriska pass through Gornja Veceriska on the way to the forest?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KVASINA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they had to pass through because there was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvasina, thank you for giving evidence in Court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And we may now move on to the first of the five witnesses to be called by Counsel Radovic and Slokovic-Glumac. So Mr. Vidovic? Does the Defence require any protective measures for these five witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: None of them? Good. All right. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you introduce yourself, please?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milutin Vidovic. I was born on the 31st of January, 1961, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where do you reside?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I reside in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What schooling have you had?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have completed secondary school, vocational school, and I am a machinist by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In 1992, can you tell us where you were employed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was employed in the Slobodan Princip Selo company, and I worked in the boiler room there until March or April, when I was sent home and I waited, but I was nonetheless registered as an employee.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you work after that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In April I worked with Ljuban Santic, my neighbour, and I rented a cafe from Pican, and we ran the cafe for three to four months.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, did you change your job?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I went to work at the market, the vegetable market.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you continue to work there until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked there until the first and second conflict. In the meantime, I went to Gornji Vitez and opened a kiosk selling foodstuffs next to the house of my sister, Marija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, you have already told us where you worked, but were you a member of the active component of the HVO at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you in any way take part in the war against the Serbs that took place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I went twice to the front line, towards the Serbs. The first time was at Slatka Voda above Novi Travnik. I went there for seven days. And the second time I went to Vlasic, once again a seven-day shift. On both occasions, I went voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was in 1992? Was it the beginning of the year, the middle of the year, or the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I went to Slatka Voda, I think it was the middle of the year. And at Vlasic, I think that was at the end of the summer, around September. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you are on the list of the active component of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And we sent this list to the Trial Chamber. Did you ever receive any remuneration from the HVO, a salary of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you in any way take part in any wartime operations, apart from the two occasions that you mentioned now, up until the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How come, then, that you are on the list? Is it an exact fact?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think the data there is exact, because I was never within the active component of the HVO until the war and after the war. Afterwards, we all moved over, up to the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So up to the 16th of April, you were not there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you went on these two occasions to the front line facing the Serbs, Slatka Voda and Vlasic, did you receive weapons and a military uniform from anybody?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On both occasions I borrowed parts of a uniform from Ante Vidovic Satko, I got a hat from him, and from Ipaca I got some boots, and from Dragan Calic, I got a rifle. And when I came back from the front, I returned this clothing and the weapon to these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who are these people? Are they people from the village, or where are they from?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they're from the village. Dragan Calic is from Nadioci, and the other two are from Santici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say that he gave you a rifle; that means that you did not have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not have a rifle up until the fall of Jajce. When the wave of refugees came into Vitez, a lot of weapons were bought and that's where I bought myself an M-48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, how much did you pay for your rifle? How expensive was it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It cost me 150 Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you buy the rifle? Where were rifles bought and sold?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the town itself. There was a wave of refugees, there was a column of tractors, and heavy duty things, and it was raining, and they asked to spend the night there. The Croats stayed there. After one or two days, they would move on and go further towards Tomislavgrad and towards Croatia. The majority of the Muslim refugees stayed in Vitez, because we noticed afterwards that there were a lot of people we didn't know, unknown people, in all the surrounding villages and in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about your own village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Santici, there were no people from Jajce. There were a few Croats -- that is to say I know they went on up to Busovaca, and the Muslims for the most part were in Ahmici, where there were about 20 or 30 people put up in one house or in various apartments or where they could. They went where they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: May we now have Prosecutor's Exhibit -- the big map of Ahmici, Number 2, the aerial photograph of Ahmici, the Prosecution Exhibit Number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vidovic, could you now please, on this aerial photograph of Ahmici, indicate the location of your house and the area of Santici.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My house is located here (indicating). The general area of Santici is this area here which you can't see on the map, and it goes this way up until here, the stadium, and stretching along this way up to the road and below the road, but that these sections -- this section here is called Gornja Zume and this area is Donja Zume, where it is all the village of Santici (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So Zume are, in fact, part of Santici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This part which follows on from Santici and which says "Ahmici" in the middle, is that the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This? You mean this (indicating)? No. This is Pirici, and Pirici borders on Santici, this way, this part here right up until the road, towards Ahmici, and Ahmici are this part here, Donja Ahmici, Gornja Ahmici (indicating). And this is Pirici, the forest and everything in that area (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say Gornji Pirici, Upper Pirici, what part of Pirici is that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said Upper Ahmici, Gornja Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But when they say Gornji Pirici, what area does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those are these houses here along the forest (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in the part that you indicated where your own house is located, was that a predominantly Muslim part or a Croat part?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was a predominantly Croatian part, just like Santici proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who were your next door neighbours, your Muslim next door neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My nearest neighbour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- he lived across the road here, (redacted), and he lived here (indicating), and the neighbours on the lower half of the road. That means that it (redacted) (redacted) up here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So they were your only neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my closest neighbours there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And on the upper part of the road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Along the upper part of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say, on the left-hand side if you're going from Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you show us Pican's cafe, the location of Pican's cafe?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pican's cafe here right by the road (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In that part there is another cafe?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the cafe of Ivo Vidovic. It is located some 20 metres away from the main road on this route towards my house, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in fact, these two cafes are next to each other?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are just divided by the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can resume usual seat now. Were there any village guards in your part of the village in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you recall when these village guards were set up, when you started to set up the village guards?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We started establishing village guards after the conflict with the Serbs. That is to say, from 1992. People organised themselves. They would leave their houses because they were afraid for their families. It was rumoured that on several occasions, in the Serbian village of Tolovici, a helicopter had landed there, and there was a the lot of looting, cars were being stolen. There were bands that went around stealing cars and storming garages to steal the cars, breaking into the garages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Up until the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the first conflict I was not on guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because I didn't have any weapons, and I would spend the whole day working at the market, from early in the morning until late at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that the village guards were set up in 1992. What part of 1992, the first half, the second half? When were they formed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the first half, that is to say that in April and May of 1992 the village guards were set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many people were included, according to your knowledge, into the village guard in your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were not many people that took part in these watches because not everybody had weapons. The people that had weapons would take part in the village guards and there were about ten of these. They were Croats. Afterwards, they were joined by the Muslims from the lower pat of the village and the village guards were manned jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who of the Muslims stood guard with the Croats in your part of the village? Did you see Muslims going out to do guard duty?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The sons – (redacted) (redacted) they would go with two Croats. I'm quoting them as an example. Then there was Braco Vrebac on one occasion, and he was with Ljuban Santic. Then there were two members from(redacted). There was Fahran Ahmic. He came from the lower part of the village and they met up at Ivo's cafe somewhere. I know that (redacted) was also included, as was his brother-in-law Strmonja Miralem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: (redacted) and Strmonja Miralem are Muslims, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you indicate on the map, please, which route did you go when you went on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We would go from the main road, taking this route towards my own house, towards Zdravko Vrebac's house, and on towards to Pirici to the Vrebac houses below the forest -- no, that's a mistake. We went this way (indicating). These are the houses. Then we would go back towards Niko Sakic's house and Ramo's house. This is the route we took for the most part (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So it means that you went from the road to the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up to my own house and then upwards towards the Vrebac's houses. Then we would go back, go towards Niko Sakic's house this way (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you became included into the village watch -- you said that you became a member after the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there an individual in your part of the village who would organise these village guards?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody existed. We would organise ourselves, and, quite simply, I would replace the people who had done guard duty. I would do that several times to give the people a chance to rest and to have a good night's sleep from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How then did you make up the shifts and how would you know who would be on guard duty the next day?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no schedules. It would be me today, you tomorrow, somebody would replace somebody else. So there was no real schedule or order in which this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you in any way linked with people who did guard duty in other parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, we were not linked up with them because each part of the village would have its own village watch around their own houses, protecting their own families, their women and children who were sleeping, their elderly folk, and their property.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the first conflict which took place on the 19th of October, 1992. Where were you on that particular day, that is to say, on that particular night?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, 1992, that day I went to work in the marketplace, and as I always did, I came home towards dusk. And I had a car, the make was a Kadett. I left the goods I had at home, and then went to Ivo Vidovic's cafe. This was sometime around 8.30 to 9.00. I don't know who was there but there were some 15 people, and somebody turned up from the direction of Busovaca towards Vitez and told us that the Muslims had placed a barricade near our cemetery at Topala. In talking about this event, I and Anto Vidovic, Pero Jelic, decided to go to the cemetery, because we were previously told that the Muslims were digging trenches on the left-hand side of the cemetery and in the cemetery itself. Fifteen days prior to that, I had erected a monument to my late mother, and I wanted to see that her tombstone had not fallen down perhaps, or that something had happened that none of us would like to see happening. About 9.00 we started out along the main road towards the cemetery, myself and Anto and Pero. We arrived at the cemetery, we went into the cemetery and we didn't find any Muslims there, nor did we notice that any trench digging was going on in the cemetery itself. However, at the turning by the cemetery, two hedgehog devices had been positioned and several anti-tank mines, and on the other side we heard thuds, as if something was being dug, and we could make out the silhouettes, the contours. I couldn't see exactly how many people were there, it was night-time, but we could make out some silhouettes. We didn't talk to anybody. We lit candles in the church at the cemetery, and returned and went to the road entering into -- which goes into Ahmici. At the entrance to Ahmici itself, some ten metres away there was another barricade that had been set up, and it was made out of wooden logs, horizontally placed logs, with two anti-tank mines. We stopped there because we recognised some local Muslims, (redacted), Pezer Ibrisim, his brother, (redacted), the driver of the bus, and there was the other Pezer. He's also a bus driver and his nickname is Scene. I think his name was Nezir. Yeah, it may be Nezir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Nezir Ahmic you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You recognised these people, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At the barricade were there people whom you didn't recognise?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from them at the barricade there were seven or eight other individuals that I didn't know. And going back, there was Asim Ahmic's son at the barricade, and he was going back with us. He was going back towards his house, because his house was also in the direction of Santici from this road going to Ahmici, and he was accompanied by a tall young man. I asked him, the young man, where he was from because I didn't know this tall young man, and he just mumbled something and said, "Well, I'm from these parts," and didn't say anything else. Then they separated and branched off going towards their own house and we went back towards Ivo Vidovic's cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The people that you saw up at the barricade, did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: and a pistol, and he was dressed in a uniform -- a guard uniform, because, in fact, he worked at the Princip factory as a guard. (redacted) had a machine gun but a new type. It was the Serbian type of submachine gun. Other people – (redacted) a hunting carbine, and the tall young man had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) and all the other people whom I didn't know had uniforms. (redacted) Princip factory guard uniform, Ibrisim was wearing civilian clothing and his brother was wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice what kind of uniforms they were wearing? Were they camouflage uniforms, new uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were all camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia, any signs of any kind on the uniforms, or didn't you notice?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly whether there were any -- whether there were insignia. I know (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened up at the barricade when you turned up there? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the one in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we reached the barricade they were behind the barricade, and there was a sort of bunker made out of some blocks, towards the right-hand corner,

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. When you say "bunkers" you meant blockades by the road?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Blocks piled up one on top of another forming a square.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in front of Ivo's cafe --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I apologise, but just tell us what you talked to them about.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked about the information that we had received, that our cemetery had been desecrated and that trench digging was going on, and so that this should not be done in -- during the course of the night, (redacted) that this wouldn't happen and we didn't want any conflict to break out because of these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you ask them why they were manning the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked – we asked(redacted) why they had these barricades put up, and he said, "Well, I don't know." He said that it was because some weapons had been seized. I don't really know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So it was a sort of retribution?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Something of the kind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You went back to Ivo Danicin's cafe, did you not, and what happened on that evening?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That evening we told them that the Muslims were not digging trenches in our cemetery, that we had talked to them and that there would be no problems there. I went home to sleep, and in the morning, I was woken up at about 4 a.m. by Dragan Vidovic, Nikica, my next-door neighbour, and he told me to get up and said the Muslims were blocking the road, and that they were not allowing anybody to pass, and that we should be awake. So I got up --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one moment. Dragan Vidovic is your neighbour, is he?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Vidovic, Nikica's son. There are five Dragan Vidovics. This was Nikica's Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mean in the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And this particular Dragan Vidovic, Nikica, had a house in Santici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is across the road from (redacted) house; that's where his house is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went with him to Anto Vidovic's house, which is right next to the stadium at Zume. Satko also got up. We were in his yard. There was fog that morning. Sometime before 5.00, a burst of fire could be heard somewhere in the direction of Ahmici. That's where it came from. And at 5.00 in the morning, you could hear some kind of music, which was very unusual for me; I had not heard such music before. It was coming from the mosque itself. They had powerful loudspeakers. And the announcement came: "Croats, surrender. This is a holy war, a jihad. You are surrounded. You stand no chance." This was followed by an explosion, and this music stopped, and this announcement. It was foggy, so we couldn't see anything. Sometime around 6.15, 6.20, I went to the house of Mirko Sakic with Dragan. I found Mirko Sakic there, Miro Pudja, Dragan Samija, Miro Samija, Miro Vidovic, Anto Vrnada, Mirko Grgic, Pero Jelic. And after us, other people came; Braco Vrebac Zdanko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All these people were residents of Zume, of that area, in Zume. Civilians, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In other words, your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please show to the Trial Chamber on this aerial photograph where exactly you went, which road you took to Mirko Sakic's house, and where that house is located.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This house is Anto Vidovic Satko's house. This is my house. I took this road here to his house. From Satko's house, when I went with Dragan, I took this road past Niko Vidovic's house, where a shelter was, (redacted), to the house of Niko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This Niko Sacic's house; please point to that, too.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is it from the Kupreskics' houses?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is about 150 metres, maybe up to 200 metres from the Kupreskic houses. If you go to Kupreskic houses, you have to take this road and arrive to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's where your neighbours were. You arrived, and what happened there? Could you hear or see anything?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 6.30, you could -- we heard shooting from the lower part of Ahmici. Later we learned that this shooting was around the cemetery itself, the Croatian cemetery. Dragan Vidovic and Zdravko Vrebac and I, since there were no Kupreskics around, went to this depression, and from there peered to see around and saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, with their wives and children, near Ivica's father's house. We approached them. I helped Zoran and Zdravko helped Mirjan to carry a child, because they also had bags with things for children. We helped them come to Mirko Sakic's house. They went on to the shelter, and I stayed at Mirko's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know to which shelter they went?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We sent them in the direction of my house. I know that Zoran's wife, Mira, was at my place, and Mirjan's wife was at Zdravko Vrebac's house, in fact in the basement of his sister's house. But she also came to my house because they were one next to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they go to their sister's?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They only stayed there very briefly. And they then went to Santici, to Zoran and Mirjan's sister's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where is their sister's house? What is their sister's name? Can you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Their sister is in Santici. It's -- Zorica is her name, and it's Anto Rajic's house. You cannot see their house on the map. It would be right here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is still Santici?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After they took their wives and children to the shelter, do you know, did they go to their sister at that time, or later? Did they tell you this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they come back to where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they came to where we were, and we were with us (sic) at Mirko's house all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened in the village on that day? You said that the shooting had started; and after that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, the population -- that is, women and children -- were moving to shelters. The ones who were close by. You could hear intense fire there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which part of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In lower Ahmici, near the cemetery, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This shooting, how long did it last? Was it intense shooting, or sporadic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: While we were helping Zoran and Mirjan carry their stuff, the shooting was intense. Later on it quieted down, and it stopped sometime in the afternoon, sometime around 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see where the shooting was going on, who was taking part in fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, we could not see from the -- from the -- our vantage point, which was behind Sakic's house. It was foggy, plus you couldn't see that area from the trees, the forest. Later on I learned that a Croat was killed there, and a Muslim; I think his name was Halid Pezer. And Andzelko Vidovic, from some unit in Busovaca -- from Busovaca, which was en route to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was this Halid Pezer a soldier? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was a military recruit. I know that he was over 18 years of age. Muslims were sending their people to near Sarajevo, to Cekrcici. This was just on the eve of these events. I know that when they were returning from Sarajevo, from Cekrcici, there was shooting. People were shooting in the air, celebrating their safe return.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You saw this Halid Pezer, and that's how you know he was a soldier? I don't quite understand what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We saw them in uniforms when they were going to Sarajevo, to Cekrcici. They were going in buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you were referring to the Muslims whom you were seeing around at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On that day, did you see any houses burning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, we only noticed that there was one fire in the lower part of the village, and later we learned that Sudzuka's house had burned down, and a barn, and Drago Josipovic's barn.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice that the Muslim population was leaving the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, behind Mirko's house, in a forest, I noticed a man and a woman leading a cow and going in the direction of upper Ahmici. At that time, Mirko, Dragan Vidovic -- I think Zoran was also with us -- and I went to this depression, and there was like a cluster of trees there, and we heard some voices around the house of Rudo Vidovic. His house was unfinished at the time. From this cluster of trees, I crawled over to see who it was. In this shelter, I saw Goga Vidovic, her mother, and I could also overhear some male voices. I spent there about a minute or two, and then I heard Goga addressing one of them by name. I realised that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were they hiding in this shelter?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the shelter, all of them. Down in this basement area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please show on these aerial photographs where Rudo Vidovic's unfinished house was?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This should be around here. We were here (Indicating). It is like an island. You see there's, like, all forest around. And see, this is the depression (Indicating). Then we went -- from there I went over to the house and then went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Gordana Vidovic talk to these people in a normal voice, like, the voices were not agitated or anything?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she talked to them in a normal voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You may be seated again. So you said that you heard shooting going on until the afternoon, and then what happened after the shooting stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the shooting stopped, we spent the rest of the day -- I believe we also spent that whole night at Mirko Sakic's house, in a shed where the wood was kept. The next day and the following days I continued to work on the market, while the Muslims who had worked in the market did not show up for three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which Muslims are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only to the Muslims from Ahmici. For instance, Alaga Ahmic, I can take him for example, because he worked with me at the marketplace. And some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did all Muslims flee the village on the 20th? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From my part of the village, nobody left, including (redacted) with his family, or Miralem Strmonja, or (redacted). Only three or four sons, one of them was quite young, so he stayed behind; only those three or four went to Pirici, to Zeir's place, because they were close with each other, and they would occasionally spend a night there. So -- but none others left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you are saying that you kept -- you saw your neighbours on the following days?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them on the following days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Muslims fled from other parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I saw some going from the lower part of the village to the upper part of the village, but I don't know where, and I didn't see anybody else leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the Muslims asked that -- in other words, I'm just asking whether the Croats asked the Muslims to turn in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Croats had asked that some four rifles be returned to them which had been taken away from them at the barricade near the cemetery. And other than that, I don't know of any other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know who asked this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would just like that some of these positions be marked on the aerial photographs. I think we will be -- we will be coming to that in the future testimony, so if I may ask the usher's assistance with that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D82/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, will you please mark -- if you can mark your own house with a circle. Where is your house located?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you now please mark the house of Mirko, that is Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you please shade the path you took from your house to Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And now from Niko Sakic's house could you show which road you take to go to the Kupreskic houses?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes. Use your magic marker to draw the line.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is this a path of some sort?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a footpath. There's no road there. From Nicko's house on there's no road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Now, please mark the position -- the location where you were on the 20th. What was that location where you said that you arrived at Niko Sakic's house and then went down into that depression?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is Niko's house (marks). This is when I helped Zoran and Mirjans' -- the family. Then I backed up this way to Niko's house, and I remained there and they continued on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were you on that day? Where did you --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Behind Niko's house to the edge of this little fort, and then you can call this an island and I was there, this cluster of trees (indicating)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does this depression have some kind of a natural cover?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a forest and there is this depression which is fairly deep, so you couldn't see from it until you reached the very edge of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you also please show where this barricade was located by the cemetery and on that road so that we can mark that too?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was right here, at the beginning of this curve, and then this is where the trenches were dug (marks), and at this intersection to the -- of the road to Ahmici (marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So one barricade by the cemetery and the other one where -- at the turn-off. And this trench which you marked, did you see that trench later on?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that trenches had been dug up, and I later learned that that is where the fighting took place, where Halid Pezer and Andjelko Vidovic were killed. It is near this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I think we can take a break right now and then move to the second part of the testimony after the break so that we keep it in one continuous whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Therefore, after that first conflict, what were the relations like between the Muslims and Croats in the village? Did you see any problems in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the first conflict the Croatian-Muslim relations became more tense, and there was a certain amount of mistrust, the one towards the others. The village guards were separated. There were separate Croat-Muslim guards and Muslim village guards, and each separate group would stand guard in front of their own houses. The people working with me at the market I felt of a certain amount of distrust towards me. You couldn't do any work together with them as you could before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents of any kind in the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In your part of the village, were there any problems with the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In my part of the village there were no problems with the Croats and the Muslims either before or after that first conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice that barricades were being set up in the village, facing the Muslim section of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On one particular evening after the first conflict, some 30 days later, one of my friends, Mirko Grgic, had a Mercedes motor car, and he had had something to drink and I got in the car with him, it was evening, around 21.30 hours, when he, with his car, turned into Ahmici. I tried to convince him not to go but he kept driving on, and he turned off by Vlatko Kupreskic's house, moving towards Gornji or Upper Ahmici. Just up above Vlatko Kupreskic's house there was a Muslim barricade, and two what we call goat devices were set up and a log across them, and there were mines, and these trestles were put up and they stopped us and our car. This was right by the house of Sead Ahmic and his father Zuhdija. At the barricade was Pezer Sesro, Pezer Ibrisim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were the people at the barricades armed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed. Zuhdija Ahmic came up to Mirko on his side, he opened the window, and he told him to go back, that he couldn't go on. Mirko went back for several metres, turned the car around and we went back the way we came. I criticized him for the whole thing, because in the evening hours, at that time, it wasn't a good idea to go into other sections of the village which were inhabited either by Muslims or by any other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you frightened on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was frightened on the occasion and said that I would never enter a car with him again, and I told him a couple of other things to boot, so that I didn't go anywhere with him any more, especially not at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, that is to say, one day before the conflict broke out in Vitez, where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day I went to work in the marketplace as I usually do and -- at the kiosk in Gornji Vitez, and at the market I saw a lot of Muslims. My friends were there too, Mirko Grgic, Anto Vrnada. I saw my brother there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What's your brother's name?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Vidovic. He was in the PZO but he was in civilian clothes on that day, and he was in the Lovac cafe with the boys from the marketplace who worked there. He was with Slovenka and Ljilja and they were sitting down at the same table together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said your brother was a member of the PZO. That is air defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was this PZO part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. The then PZO was a mixed defence corps. There were Muslims and Croats there, and anti-aircraft guns because of the Serbian planes that had previously been bombing Busovaca and the factory in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time they were also guarding the SPS, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did your brother give you any information, as he was connected through the PZO with the HVO, that something could take part -- place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My brother conveyed nothing to me on that day. He gave me no information whatsoever, and I don't think he knew anything either, because he stayed there that day drinking, and then he went off to Stari Vitez to the fire brigade building there where he spent the night in a Muslim house. And I don't know -- never knew anything more about him and I don't to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know who took your brother away from that Muslim house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Hodzic Safeta Sijo, Hodzic Safeta, his brother-in-law was living in the house with him, I don't know his exact name, Abdic Bugar, and his nickname was Cicko, and two other policemen, and I learnt this later on, that they were -- their native village was Preocica, and they had been working in that part of Vitez when the command was in the fire brigade building there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The individuals that took your brother away, were they members of the military police of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you find his body later?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well then. So you went home and you had no information?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I had no information. I stayed at home with my family, I went to bed and went to sleep, and in the morning at around 4.00 a.m. I was woken up by Slavko Papic, who told me to get up so that as many people should be awakened up as possible because of the possible unrest or conflict. I didn't really understand him very well but something of that sort. So I got dressed and I went out into the road in front of my house and came to my brother's house. I knocked at his door because I didn't know that my brother had stayed up there. I thought that he had come home to spend the night there. So I banged on his door; nobody opened. Then I started thinking, perhaps somebody had woken him up earlier and he left earlier because he was in the PZO, so maybe he had left earlier. So I decided to go towards Niko Sakic's house. On the road there --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us whether you met anybody on your way?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were other people from the village, and behind Slavko Papic's house I met Anto Vidovic Satko and Ivica Vidovic, his brother. We talked a little bit and we went to Niko Vidovic's house together, which was where the shelter was, and they stayed out in the road and I went up to Niko Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you show us on the large map which way you went when you met Ivo Vidovic? Which way were you going when you met Vidovic and Satko? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is where I met Anto Vidovic Satko and Ivica Vidovic, and we were moving towards this house here, that is Niko Vidovic's house and their uncle's house, and they stayed there whereas I went on towards Niko Sakic's house (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons with you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have an uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. All I had was a sort of multicoloured jacket, just the top part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When Slavko Papic woke you up and told you to go out, that there could be problems, did he tell you exactly what was going to happen, and where you should go and what you should do?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. All he did was to wake me up. He told me from the window; I stayed in the house. I didn't meet him any more when I left the house. Quite simply, I went towards Sakic's house instinctively, because in the first conflict that's where we went, because there was a sort of -- it was a sort of shelter. There was a shelter by Niko Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you went to Niko Sakic's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is where the house is (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any people there already when you turned up?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I met Pero Jelic there, Miro Vidovic was there already, Miro Pudja, Dragan Samija, and the other inhabitants came as well, Mirko Grgic, Anto Branada, because his house is near Sakic's house. Those are the houses there (indicating). So we sort of lost ourselves en route, because nobody knew anything. Nobody could give us the proper information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the people you mentioned were people from the surrounding houses, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Apart from the people that you have just enumerated, the neighbours you mentioned a moment ago, did you see anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 5.00, from the direction of Sutrine Kuce and the Kupreskic houses, Zoran, his wife, his children, Mirjan with his wife and their children turned up, and Mirjan's mother-in-law, and they stopped by Mirko and me, and they stopped by Mirko's house. I thought they would be going to my house, but Zoran, with his wife, went to my house with his wife and children. And his people stayed behind at my house, whereas Mirjan and his children and his wife, they were in the shelter right next to my own house. That is the house here, right across from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Whose house is that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is Jozo Bredsa's (phoen) house, and his son-in-law. He's a Macedonian, I think. The man never lived there. He lived abroad somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. So you saw them taking away their families, taking them towards Zume; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the route. It goes from Niko Sakic's house towards my own house. After their departure, a group of about 30 well-armed individuals came up. They were masked. They had something black on their faces. It was still morning, and rather dark; it wasn't clearly visible, but they had some paint over their faces and were wearing black uniforms. They had camouflage uniforms as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were armed with automatic rifles, and I saw that they were very well armed, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles. I think one of them had a Heckler; that is a rifle with a rather long barrel. And they also had RPGs on their backs; once again, long barrels, wide barrels. And they were wearing the belts for ammunition for automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Would you tell us what RPGs are?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They are hand-propelled rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the wraps you mentioned, what are they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They are sort of bandoleers, with ammunition for automatic rifles. In fact they are metal boxes, metal boxes with the ammunition inside, and these can be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were they carrying these wraps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They carried them in front. They were sort of hung round their necks. And they were also camouflage, like the uniforms themselves, the same colour -- they matched the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they have anything on their heads?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They had helmets, and some sort of black caps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything else on them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They had white belts. I saw a couple of rifle holders. They were -- and they had light blue bands on their shoulders, sort of like some sort of epaulet. They all had these light blue bands. Passing by us, some of them asked for a match, matches. I'm not a smoker, so I wasn't able to supply them with any matches. I recognised Mirjan Santic as they passed by us, who did not have black on, black paint on his face, but he just had a scarf around his neck.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How do you know Mirjan Santic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known Mirjan for a long time, because Mirjan lives in the village of Santici; he lives in the part of the village where Zoran and Mirjan's sister lives, in the centre of Santici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that means that he is a native of Santici, and he also resides in Santici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can his house be seen on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Because it's in the lower half. It's a newly constructed house, and his parents' house is above his, and you can't even see their house on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw on several of them the insignia of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you had seen the white belts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw white belts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you conclude from that fact?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I concluded that it was a military police unit. I knew Mirjan from earlier on, and I knew that he was a member of the military police, and therefore I concluded that it was a military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How do you -- did you feel when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were frightened, all of us, because suddenly out of the dark, a lot of well-armed individuals confronted us. They were wearing black; they looked like something out of a ninja film. And we were petrified when we saw them. Mirko was standing beside me, and we just looked at each other, and we didn't know what to say. I was quite lost at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you show us the direction from which they came to Niko Sakic's house? What direction?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to point on the map, over there, the big map, or on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please point to the location on the big map.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Indicating) They appeared from this direction, going towards Niko Sakic's house. It is the same route that I took, and which Zoran and Mirjan had taken away their wives and children. They went along the same route.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did this group of -- where was this group of people going?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
