utterances.text: The group of people went towards this valley, and we lost sight of them. They went towards the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you hear any shooting at that time, or was there nothing to be heard yet?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was no shooting to be heard at that precise moment. A little later, when they had left, shooting was heard --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please; let me ask you something else. When they left, did you see the Kupreskics anywhere around?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when they left, several minutes after them, Zoran and Mirjan turned up from this direction and they went with Mirko Sakic and Dragan Vidovic, Dragan Samija. They went off to this valley here, following them; they went off after them. Several minutes later -- and I stayed here waiting for Mirko Grgic and Anto to turn up, and Zoran Kupreskic came once again. And he had Didaks -- two wives and four children who had been put up in the house of Ivica's brother. They didn't want to leave right away. They only left later, and Zoran went with them in this direction. And I, together with Anto Vrnada, Mirko Grgic, and Miro Pudja, as well as Miro Samija, we went to Bijela Zemlja, up here, and we kept guard over the shelter of Niko Vidovic by Niko Sakic's house below Bijela Zemlja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that Mirko Sakic and Mirjan Kupreskic -- and who else did you mention? That they went to the valley, to the depression there. Who else was with them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Samija was with them. Dragan Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which Dragan Vidovic is that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dragance, the one that woke me up. Niko's Dragan. And some other young men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see where they put up?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were located below this forest in a depression there, a valley. And you can't see out of that depression. You can't -- because it's surrounded by forest, so it's a sort of natural depression protected on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is that the depression where you were in the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not that valley or depression. That was another one. It went straight on from Niko Sakic's house. That's where we were on the occasion of the first conflict, whereas they went left now. And that depression forms a sort of triangle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is the depression situated in such a way that it represents a natural shelter?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is closed on all sides, and only a mortar shell could fall there. But no bullets could penetrate that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down again now. When Zoran left with the refugees on the second occasion --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- at that time, that is to say, when did you hear the first bout of shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first shooting could be heard before Zoran passed by me with the Didak people from the lower part of the village, around the mosque, in the lower section. Then there was shooting from several directions, and you couldn't tell where the shooting was coming from. There were bullets flying by from all directions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where could shooting -- in what other parts could the shooting be heard?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was shooting by the Kupreskic houses themselves, in the lower part of the village. Some of it was a little further off around the cemetery, the lower part of the village, and around the Kupreskic houses, in the central part of Ahmici, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you indicate on the map the position where you saw Mirjan, and Vidovic, and Sakic, and where you yourself were. Would you mark that in on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On this same map, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, another one. We're going to hand you another map, so that we don't get things mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: By using a Magic Marker, will you please put a letter "A" at the spot where you saw that Mirjan Kupreskic, and Vidovic, and Sakic were positioning themselves. I cannot see it very well. What if you use a black marker?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps another colour, yes. (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is the area where there's no forest?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So when you said that you went to this area which you called Bijela Zemlja, can you mark that area, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with the letter "B". Was that area also somehow protected?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That area was somehow protected, because again there was -- the ground was settling down, because there used to be a mine in there; then the mine was abandoned, and then it was starting to cave in, and then sort of these depressions were formed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please again circle the house of Niko Sakic, and mark it with the number "1".

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether people came to take shelter in Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know what people these were, from which area they came?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These were people, men, women, children, who lived around the Sakic houses; that is, the Grgic families and the others took shelter in Niko Vidovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you please mark Niko Vidovic's house which was also used as shelter. And mark it with number "2" please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So your house was also used by some people to shelter?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was in your house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In my house there were Mirja Kupreskic, Zoran's wife, with her children; later on, the two Didak women with four children also came there, my wife, one of my children, Jasna Safradin and her child, Kristina. And when I came home around 7.30, I saw Mirjan's wife as well. She was working around the stove. I guess she was preparing food for children. I didn't stay long, five or ten minutes, and then went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you please mark your house so that we see where else the civilians were located. And mark it with number "3"?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you also mark the house of Jozo Vrebac; that is, his son-in-law. And mark it with number "4" please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these local residents, that is, women and children, were also sheltering in that house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of people in that house, because the lower part of the house was dug into the ground. Also there was more space than in my house. So that there were many more women and children there than at my place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In these four houses, were mostly women and children from that area, that is, from Ahmici, Santici and Pirici accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The position which you chose, you said that it was a natural -- some kind of -- it was some kind of a depression due to the caving in, so it was a natural shelter?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and above us we had dense oak forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did you go there? Did somebody tell you to go to that place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody told me to go there. We simply went there up from those shelters, so the four or five of us, Mirjan, Zoran, were there to protect a potential advance of the Muslim forces towards the shelters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So during the day, did you go over to them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went over there a couple of times, to where they had taken shelter in that depression, and so I saw them all there. I talked to them. There was shooting. There's a natural path around the area where the old mine was, to where they were. You just went through the thicket and you reached them. The distance between myself and them was somewhere between 70 and 100 metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you went there, who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Mirjan Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, Mirko Sakic, Dragan Vidovic, and Dragan Samija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see whether they were shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not shooting because you couldn't even shoot from that position anywhere else because it is a depression. You can only shoot up in the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see what happened when you went over to them? Did you see what was going on in the other parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Ahmici you could still hear intense shooting. You could see that houses were on fire. I couldn't determine the exact positions, because they were burning in the area of the Kupreskic houses and then also in the lower sections of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did you see -- how did you recognise that they were burning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the smoke, I heard crackling sounds, and you see light and a large plume of smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In this part of the village where you were between those two depressions, you also said that you went back home; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the way there and in the area where you were moving, was there fighting going on there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I went home at 7.30, around that time, as I was passing by Niko Vidovic's shelter, on the road I met (redacted), his son-in-law Miralem Strmonja, Anto Vidovic Satko, all four of them had rifles and they were standing in the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The two persons you just mentioned, Ramo Bilic and Miralem Strmonja, were they Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims. Their house is directly across from the shelter of Niko Vidovic. And when I reached them, they were also -- they had also just arrived. Ivica and Anto were with them, and we said to them, "Don't shoot. We're not going to shoot either." So we -- they said, "So, neighbours, what is going on?" And they didn't know either. So Anto Vidovic said to the other two to move their women and children to the shelter where our women and children were, that is in Niko Vidovic's house. So we talked a little bit and I went on, continued to my house. On the way back I did not see them in the road. I met Anto and he said that they were already in the shelter, together with the women and children, that even Zijad Bilic, Ramo's brother who was not on the road at that time, that he and his wife and children were also -- that they had also taken shelter in that shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And these people were all accommodated in this Croatian house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, along with all the other Croatian women and children who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anything happen to those people on that day or did Croats protect them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That day they were protected by local Croatian residents and nothing bad happened to them. I later learned, I didn't see this, that they were taken to the railroad station where there were other Muslim families and that they were transferred to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And they all survived?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they all survived, but only Zijad Bilic, Ramo's brother, was killed, I learned later, during the subsequent fighting at Buhine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So he was killed at Buhine Kuce. That was in January of '94; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did something happen on that day in that part of the village where you stayed, or was this a situation the entire day?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was the situation throughout the day. We went back and forth trying to get some information. We couldn't get any information. Nobody from outside provided any information, so we just stayed in that area. Some of us went to their homes to get some food and would come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On that first day, until what time could you hear shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that first day it -- the shooting went on until about the end of the day, till the dusk, and then it stopped and it resumed the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The second day, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day I remained in that same area, and on that day I again went several times to Sakic's, and Kupreskic's, and Grgic's and Dragan Vidovic's. We commented but not having any real information, we just realised that there was some fierce fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you hear the shooting the second day also?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could also hear shooting, but it had already moved to the middle Ahmici, so you can't hear it as much in the lower part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there shooting -- could the shooting be heard from the Upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, shooting could be heard from the Upper Ahmici, but would I say from the other side near Krc. There is an area around Nadoici going this way that is called Krc, and some bullets even flew in our direction. The distance between there was just about four or five hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did something happen to civilians, that is the women and children who were in the shelters on that second day? Did you have any -- do you know whether they were moved to another shelter or somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that some of them moved. I don't know who went from Niko Sakic's basement more towards Niko Vidovic's house, but I don't know who was involved there. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know that women and children went to Rovna?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. Only later when I came home I found my wife and child, Zoran's wife and children, and they told me that somebody had said that between Mahala and Krtina there is a creek there at Mahala, and this area is part of Santici, that a group of Muslims had passed by and that they should take shelter, and that the majority of residents went to Rovna, but my wife and Zoran's wife and children remained in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The third day what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the third day three or four men came. They were wearing uniforms. They didn't have any -- they didn't wear any paint or anything, but I didn't know them. I know that they were military policemen. I concluded that from their uniforms and insignia. And it would be -- they told us to follow us -- to follow them to Pirici, which we did, very reluctantly, because from the area where we were there was an open area, and there were some natural shelters, little depressions, and we took shelter there. We sort of followed them along. At about the area where Gavro Vidovic's house, they stopped. We came and from -- downhill from Gavro -- Barin Gaj. There was a lot of shooting, so we were just looking for some kind of a shelter. There was like a hedge and there was a -- was a natural depression. It was seven or eight metres deep. It's called Usijak. We again took shelter there until the dusk came. Just around dusk, about 15 civilians arrived with two or three rifles, poorly dressed. I know them. They were from Vitez. They were deployed around -- along this depression, and Gavro Vidovic's house to Strmonja's house and further up towards the Upper Ahmici. So they just positioned us there, arranged us there, and left us there. We felt like lost children. They left --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This didn't -- this didn't get into the record. Were these people from Vitez which you said were poorly armed and poorly dressed, did they come on their own or did somebody bring them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were brought there. They were brought there by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And they were brought there on the third day to --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were brought there on the third day to this defence line in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you just point on the map where this line of defence was deployed, the one in Pirici? Where is Barin Gaj?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is Barin Gaj here (indicating). This is the area of Zume (indicating). This is the natural depression that opens to the left and right, and the line of defence was put up here, and then here up to Gavro Vidovic's house, through this orchard, down there near Strmonja's house here, and here next to these fields (indicating), and then later on. I don't know how it was in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the line was really in Pirici, not in Barin Gaj?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In Barin Gaj there were Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the line of defence was below Barin Gaj?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you were brought to Barin Gaj and deployed you there, from where were you shot at? You said there was intense fire coming from there.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The shooting came from Barin Gaj in the direction of Gavro Vidovic's house. So it is here, from these fields here in this direction, and we were here (indicating). So from here you could cover this area and this area (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If you can just mark on the map -- aerial photograph of Ahmici, if you can just draw in or mark the positions to which you were brought.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the line remain like that with very few movements until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did you stay on this line of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Between three and three and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said -- sorry. Do you know, in the days -- those three days when you went back home before you were deployed at the line, whether the house of -- houses of your neighbours, and I'm talking about the (redacted), were they intact or were they burned down at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were all intact. (redacted) was still intact, was never burned down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: (redacted) with you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But (redacted) subsequently burned down. I was told this by my late father, that three young men whom he did not know, wearing military police uniforms, came by and he overheard them saying they would torch the Muslim house. He said, "Don't do it, guys. You see, we have had a lot of refugees. We don't have places to put up people. We can put Croats in there, or refugees." They told him to shut up, that they would just shoot him. So he withdrew, and they proceeded to torch the lower floor of the house. And when they left he -- my father said that Jozo Vidovic, and Jozo Lovric and he tried to put out the fire so that only the lower floor burned, the fire didn't spread to the whole house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So these are Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that your father -- your brother disappeared in Old Vitez, that is in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And that in the area called Gornji Vitez or Upper Vitez your sister also lived?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My sister has a house there. She called me and miraculously the telephones were working. She called my wife and she said that I should come. I still had a kiosk up there and I had merchandise there which she said I should take. When I arrived there I saw that the yard was full. And they had a warehouse there, and I saw a large number of Muslims, men, women and children, about 30 persons were put up in that storage space.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did your sister take care of these people there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed there for about a full month, and then some of those who wanted to go to Travnik, my brother-in-law Nikola Banic went with them to UNPROFOR and he helped transport them to Stari Travnik, whereas the two younger Muslim men, they were military fit, UNPROFOR did not agree to take them to Stari Travnik, Old Travnik. They said that they were taking women, children and the wounded. So Nikola brought them back to his house, they slaughtered a chicken, they -- they bandaged an arm and a head of one of them, they put blood on these bandages, and so they pretended they were wounded and UNPROFOR took them. And a family stayed with Nikola about two and a half months. It was a husband, wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these families, because these were two families.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of them were called Alihodza. If I can just --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was it Topcic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Topcic. They were undertakers locally. So there were two families, in fact. And also Blaz had a shelter and another 20 or 30 Muslims were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one more detail. Do you remember Zoran Vidovic's wedding in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I remember Zoran Vidovic's wedding. He went -- he was from Kruscica but his wedding took place at the Lovac hotel, and it is -- the byroad doesn't go through Vitez, but is a byroad by the petrol pump belonging to Kraocic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us when the wedding took place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The wedding took place sometime in December 1992, between the first and second conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember who played and sang at the wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nedzad Barucija sang.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what is Nedzad Barucija?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He is a Muslim. He's a Muslim. Fahran Ahmic, another Muslim; Mirjan Kupreskic, you know that he's a Croat; Zdravko Vrebac was a Croat; and there was another Serb who played the guitar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That was the composition or group that Mirjan Kupreskic used to sing and play with frequently?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a sort of band. Zoran would play with them sometimes on larger occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there a lot of Muslims present at the wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, a couple of Serbs at the wedding. And those Serbs still live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened to Zoran Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Vidovic was killed in his family house. He died in his family house. On the first day, a sniper hit him through the window. And all his people had moved and are now in Croatia, somewhere near Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That means that he was killed in the house in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the lower road towards Kruscica. There are two roads leading into Kruscica. It was the lower road that his house was situated on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I am now going to let you look at some data pertaining to Zoran Vidovic to tell me if the data is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher hand the document round, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your brother is also Zoran Vidovic, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you have a death certificate for your brother?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I can have it issued -- I can get it, because I know that it exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Here it states that it is Zoran Vidovic, killed on the 16th of April, 1993, in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: His father was Ivica, and he was born in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When was your brother born?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of November, 1963. And the father is Anto.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have completed my examination of the witness. And I should like these exhibits to be tendered into evidence, and I don't have any numbers for the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers are D82/2 to D84/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection? All right. They are admitted into evidence; thank you. Counsel Radovic? No? And any cross-examination by other counsel? Mr. Pavkovic, may I ask you whether any other Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we can then move to the Prosecution: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, good afternoon to you. My name is Michael Blaxill. I am one of the prosecutors here working on this particular case. I do have a few questions I would like to put to you as a result of your testimony here this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Firstly I would say that you stated you served in the conflict against the Serbs on two occasions in the front lines for the HVO. When you completed those periods of duty, did you remain in the reserve of the HVO, even if you were not in the active component?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I completed the seven-day shift on both the first and the second occasion, up at the front line towards the Serbs, I was not in any kind of unit after that. I had no weapons, I had no duties, no assignments, nothing. So the clothing that I wore on the occasion I returned because it was borrowed, and I did likewise with the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Had you in fact been a volunteer for those two seven-day periods?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you returned back home after the second one, did they say anything to you about whether you could or should volunteer again, or would they call upon you in the future? Were you left with any kind of parting instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you aware of any mechanism that the HVO had to contact people and call them up to go and serve in the ongoing conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you returned to, I should say, your normal work; and in fact in the earlier stages of 1992, you did not join the village guard. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when, about -- could you refresh my memory: When, about, was it that you did join up with the village guards to assist in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Jajce, when I got some weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And from that point forward, with your own weapon -- which I believe was an M-48 rifle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You then joined in with the local village guard; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I joined them on several -- just several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On those occasions were they still functioning as a joint guard between the Muslim and the Croat members of the village community?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: They had already separated into Croat and Muslim guards in their own parts of the village? Is that correct, then?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's true to say, is it not, sir, that there were no incidents of tension or difficulty, were there, between yourselves, as a Croat ethnic village guard, and your Muslim ethnic village guard in the same village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this part of the village where I lived, there weren't any problems. They stood guard around their own houses; we stood guard around our own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you aware of any kind of mechanism to communicate with other village guards or other -- perhaps other Croat village guards in other parts of the area? Saying something had happened, did you have any lines of communication at all?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, only on the next day, if, for example, I would meet somebody from another part of the village, we could talk and discuss matters. But we didn't have any lines of communication, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there anybody else you could contact in case something more serious happened, like a local HVO representative, or an army commander? Was there anybody like that in the neighbourhood whom you could have spoken to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. Just the police, the police station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Are you aware of a gentleman by the name of Mr. Nenad Santic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Nenad Santic was in fact a local figure within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you aware of the presence of Mr. Nenad Santic in -- I'm jumping forward in time, but in fact in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Have you even ever heard that Mr. Nenad Santic was in a position to give instructions to people in the HVO locally, or in -- or even people who had been in the village guard, to carry out certain duties? Had you ever heard that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He could not order them. He was not any kind of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. I can move on to October of 1992, where you have indicated, I believe, that things were getting -- had already got difficult between Muslim and Croat inhabitants in the region. Is that a fair comment, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking about the first conflict, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I am indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Between us local inhabitants and the Muslims from Ahmici, there were no conflicts at all then, either. But I had heard that the Busovaca -- some kind of Busovaca unit went to Jajce, and that the road was blocked at our cemetery in Donji or lower Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you have indicated there were relatively few people manning this barricade; is that correct? I think you've mentioned about 15 people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that there were about 15 people at the barricade at the entrance towards Ahmici. Whereas down there, by our cemetery, I cannot give you an exact figure, exactly how many men there were, because I saw quite a number of silhouettes in the course of the night, but I wasn't able to either count them or see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you weren't able to see or count the numbers, and you're not prepared to assess; that's very fair. Thank you, sir. So at the entrance to Ahmici, the particular barricade you say had about 15 people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it true in fact that the conflict as it evolved, between members of the HVO and the people at the respective barricades, involved HVO forces from outside that were trying to travel through the region? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that there was a conflict between the people who wanted to pass through and the people who were at the barricades at our cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. You also indicated, I believe, that at both barricades you say there were anti-tank mines present; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Had you in fact arrived -- or had daylight arrived when you went to observe this? Or was it still dark?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to Ahmici, by the house on the left-hand side, there was a light outside that was burning, that was on. And at the entrance to the cemetery, we passed right by the hedgehog devices and the barricade, so we saw that on the road too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What sort of weather conditions did you have at that time? Was it misty, was it raining, was it clear?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning it was foggy, when the first conflict broke out. It was dense fog, and you couldn't see anything much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've given certain names of people whom you've identified as local Muslims manning the checkpoint or barricades. How close did you come to those particular barricades, in order to recognise these people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stopped at the barricade in Ahmici, and I talked to those people who were standing around right by me, half a metre or a metre away from me. We were standing around in a sort of circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So, clearly, they were people you were close to, you could see, and you could describe obviously how they were armed and so forth, as you have done so. May I --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you were asked about whether you had -- saw any insignia, but you stated you couldn't remember any insignia on the clothing worn by those people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly they had some insignia, but I'm not -- I didn't really see them. We knew that they had BH insignias, the Croats had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were the people that you had named in connection with being the Muslims manning, let's say, the barricade at the entrance to Ahmici, were any of those people local village guard people, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think they were, except (redacted), whom I knew very well. He was in the police, the Muslim police, which was stationed in Stari Vitez. But his house is there, and so he was there, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I'm sorry; would this be a convenient time for a break? A 15-minute break?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's as convenient as any time, Your Honour. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, if I may return, we were talking about the night of the 19th to the 20th of October of 1992, and I believe that just before you went home to bed you said that you spoke to the people at the barricade, at the entrance to Ahmici, and they made reference to retribution for some seized weapons. Did you have any further idea as to what he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You went home to sleep and were awoken the following morning, or later that morning at about 04.00 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you say another hour went by and then on that foggy morning you heard a burst of fire at around 5.00 from the direction of Ahmici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A little before 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You then suggest that there was a broadcast heard on a loudspeaker requesting surrender of Croats and that you were "surrounded and you had no chance." You say that that is so and that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the mosque. The loudspeakers were on the mosque in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were those the only loudspeakers that were in the village of Ahmici, the ones on the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think they were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You decided then clearly to seek appropriate shelter for your family. If I may ask, what prompted you to go across to Mr. Mirko Sakic's house to seek such shelter when, from what you described, there were other shelters, like Mr. Vrebac's shelter, much closer to your home? Why would you go further away for that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before this second conflict I had a rifle -- are we talking about the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: First conflict, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I see. I went to Sakic's house with Dragan Vidovic. I don't know why myself why, I just went along that road because I knew that there were the village guards there as well, and perhaps to inform myself quite simply, to get some information as to the events that were going on, although I don't -- I didn't learn anything from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe, unless I have made the note wrongly, you did take your family with you and have them shelter at Sakic's house, is that right, or not on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You took down the note wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. So where were your wife and family at that time when you went across to Sakic's house that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In my own house. They stayed in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On that particular day you did see, did you not, Mr. Zoran Kupreskic and his family?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: , in fact, they went on back towards your house from meeting you near Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, by Ivica's father's house, because Zdravko, and I, and Dragan Vidovic started off to meet them, and they had still not -- the shooting had started and they had still not come out of that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. So you went, if you like, forward towards the homes of the Kupreskic family and met them, and then they came back, is that right, if I'm getting the movement correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we met at his uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you remain in that area basically for the rest of the day, the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see either Mr. Zoran Kupreskic or, indeed, Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic, for that matter, during the course of the rest of that day?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were there by -- at Niko Sakic's house, together with the other group of locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were they, in fact, armed and sort of kind of standing guard as one gains the impression you were doing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did they remain in the same position or that same location for the whole of the day, until the shooting stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The whole day we were around Niko Sakic's house, and then we went down to that little island in the middle of the depression down there, and I went to Mirko's newly built house because I had heard voices. Then I returned up to them -- to the island. So that was the movement. The depression -- between the depression and Niko Sakic's house, up and down and a bit along the road by Niko's house. We sat there. There was a sort of a woodshed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you, however, in company with one another, in their company for the whole of the day or did you separate for periods of time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from time to time I would go home, they were there, but for the most part we spent practically the whole day all together. One of us would leave from time to time but for a very brief period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you remember any particular time of day when, say, Mr. Zoran Kupreskic left the little group of you for any period? Can you recall any times of day when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Zoran left with some of the Muslims to see about something, to Miro's. I think that was in the afternoon sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say that you yourself went back to your home. Can you recall the kind of time of day you did that? Was it late morning, afternoon? Can you give an hour?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was sometime during the course of the morning. I can't tell you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We come to the afternoon of the 20th of October, 1992, and I believe you said that somewhere around 4.00 the shooting ceased. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there anything from where you were that you could see of the participants in the exchange of shooting? Could you see any of the forces involved from where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have made reference to, on that day, the house of a Sudzuka being on fire, and I believe that that name is a nickname of a Mr. Mehmed Ahmic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you actually see that house on fire that day, or did you just see smoke or the appearance of fire from the direction of that house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just saw smoke, and I thought that there was burning coming from the direction of that house but I couldn't actually see the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Does the same thing apply in respect of your reference to the barn of Mr. Drago Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, on the 21st of October, after this incident, you, in fact, went back to work, as I believe you said.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You said that the Muslims from the area didn't turn up to work for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Maybe you heard this subsequently, but is it true that a number of Muslims, a considerable number, had actually left Ahmici on the date of the 20th when that action took place? Were you subsequently aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I -- I got to know that they returned after a few days as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any factors that particularly influenced their return, any gestures by the Croat population or authorities? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that in the school in Ahmici they discussed some reconciliation and an easing of tensions, because none of the local inhabitants on either side had taken part in that first conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall anybody who, say, on the Croat side was present at those discussions at the school?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think Zoran Kupreskic was there and Niko Sakic. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Clearly from what you say, Mr. Vidovic, you were not involved in those talks, so maybe you don't have knowledge of this, but were you aware of any of the terms that were then agreed at that meeting at the school? Did this become in any way public knowledge or knowledge amongst the community?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was rumoured that -- that some rifles that had been taken which were to be returned, taken away from some Croats. I think there were four rifles, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's what you recall hearing, but if I can put it this way to you, sir: The issue of returning over some weaponry by Muslims to Croats clearly was discussed at that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, ever see any kind of document in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may just have one moment, I would like to make an inquiry of my team regarding this particular document for a second, Your Honours. Thank you, I'm obliged for your indulgence, Your Honours. Thank you. Mr. Vidovic, are you familiar of the signature of Mr. Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an objection to make with regard to the conduct of the Prosecutor. He's quite obviously presenting a document that was previously rejected, not accepted as evidence, for which we do not have a source, and the witness who brought the document and the testimony was not adopted. That is to say, it was interrupted. That paper which he wishes to present the witness with is not an exhibit. So as this has not been accepted as evidence, that it cannot be presented to this witness either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, firstly, my question about the signature was really, firstly, to ascertain the propriety of even endeavouring to put a certain document to a witness, because without a certain foundation for that it is pointless to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The document is, in fact, I see, marked as Exhibit 313 with the translation 313/A. The issue, I believe, relates to a witness whose evidence -- the evidence came in the case in-chief. I'm not sure whether the person was protected. I'll just have that checked before I mention a name, but I understand that the statement had not been served within the requisite period of time and was then either rejected or withdrawn. The document was a document that was introduced in connection with that, and ---well, it's a matter as to whether the document itself is acceptable as an exhibit. If not, it would have to be properly served in the course of putting documents in cross-examination in another way. I'm not referring to the testimony of the person whose statement or whose testimony was withdrawn or rejected, but simply one of the documents that was put into court. I am entirely to be guided by your ruling, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may proceed with your question about whether the witness is able to recognise the signature. But it is a general question, and a sort of preliminary question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed, because the whole issue may be moot if the answer is a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I ask you that question again, sir: Do you in fact recognise the signature of Mr. Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That answers our question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe you stated that the situation with regard to relations between Muslims and Croats in the community did become more tense and worsened after that first conflict; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So much so that, if I can use the expression, it developed that certainly at night time it was wise not to go to different parts of the villages?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Like your other unfortunate experience you described with Mr. Grgic in his car?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've also referred to a considerable apparent increase in crimes, particularly to do with car theft and so forth. Can you tell us anything more about the types or groups of people who were doing this? Were they by chance in any form of uniformed groups? Were they Muslim groups, or Croat groups? Can you give me some idea?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These were mixed groups: Simply put, men who had no regard for peace, who had been involved in criminal activities even before. In my view, they were hiding behind uniforms and engaged in these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So basically you're saying, sir, that these people were, however, putting on uniforms; they were going in uniformed groups, albeit performing basically criminal activities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, there were civilians, too, who performed these acts. But it was mixed. Some were in uniforms; some were without uniforms. But they all carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: This obviously -- you say you obviously then maintained your village guards to protect the local population in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, on the 15th of April of 1993, you were, I believe you said, at work and then went home in the normal way?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You had -- I'm sorry; I didn't mean to talk over your response. You went to bed in the normal way; you had no fears of impending war or anything like that when you went to bed that night?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not think that something like that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then Mr. Slavko Papic woke you up at 4.00 in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you -- you seem very positive about that time, sir, at 04.00. I mean, how did you verify that it was 4.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that it was still dark, and as I was coming down, I passed through the kitchen, saw the clock, and saw that it was around 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. And what -- how had Mr. Papic woken you? Had he telephoned, or had he knocked on the door, or how did he wake you up?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He knocked on the door of my family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Obviously he alerted you to take some action, but do you remember more accurately what he actually said? Did he say what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That night I'd slept on the top floor, and when he knocked on the door, my window is above the door. I looked, saw it was him. He told me to get up, to come out, that we should be awake because of potential trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So that was all he said to you, a potential of trouble?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you form any particular thought when he said that? I mean, did that make you think of any particular type of trouble, as to what it might be?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the first conflict, I thought that a conflict could break out between the Muslims and us, because the Serbs at that time were more in the area of Vlasic and in the direction of Sarajevo. They were not in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you formed a conclusion at that time; you thought it might be a Croat/Muslim problem that would be the trouble?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Slavko Papic: Did he have any particular connections with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You think not? I will just put one suggestion to you that's been heard by this chamber, that he was in fact locally the commander of the HVO for Zume, for that small area. Does that ring any bell with your memory? Or do you still say that you don't recall that, or don't know?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a local commander for Zume. But during the war, he was appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. By using the expression "during the war," do you mean after the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the 16th. In fact, I think it was a month passed before Slavko was appointed commander. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up for me, sir; I'm obliged to you. It was now at 4.00 in the morning; you get up, presumably you woke your family, and you got everybody dressed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you then leave the house immediately that you were up and ready? Or did you stay in your home for a little while?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I got ready, took my rifle, M-48, and I went out of the house. So I stayed in for about five or ten minutes. My family stayed behind in the house, awake. I went by my brother's house, knocked on the door; I couldn't wake anybody up. Then I went to the Sakics' house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there; thank you. What time do you recall that you left the house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. I believe it was before 4.10, maybe around 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how long do you think it took to get to your -- you say your brother-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your brother's house; I'm sorry. What time do you think you got there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those are houses one next to the other, 30 metres away, perhaps, in the direction towards Sakic's house, not the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From there, would you say where you went again?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then I took the road towards Niko Vidovic's shelter, and then to Sakic's house. Along the way I met Anto Vidovic and Nikica Vidovic, and I just exchanged a couple of words with them. Then as we walked together, we passed Niko Vidovic's shelter. They went there, and I continued on to Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What time do you recall arriving at Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Between 4.20 and 4.30; somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Sakic's house, at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was not inside the house; I was in front of the house. I don't know exactly. The shooting in Ahmici had started, and then I went with the group to Bijela Zemlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At what time do you think then you arrived there? Was this sometime after 5.00, say, 5.15? Something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you said you moved on from Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say the exact time when I left Sakic's house to Bijela Zemlja. That was later. The shooting had already started in Ahmici. What time exactly it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was it shortly at around that time that you then encountered Mr. Zoran and Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic with their families?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. After Zoran passed with the Didak family, I was waiting. Anto Vrnada and Mirko -- and Zoran passed as I was waiting. He was taking with him the Didaks' family. And then we proceeded on to Bijela Zemlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall when you got there, what time you got there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I did not have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give any kind of guess as to how long it took you? Was it five minutes, or ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I went to Bijela Zemlja, or before? Several minutes. Two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Right. Do you recall how much later you encountered the Kupreskic families, and they went to seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You feel that it was around 5.00 that that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Taking into account you weren't wearing a watch, what made you think it was around 5.00, then, particularly?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The basis that -- time I spent at Sakic's house, which was about half an hour; perhaps 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So from that location you described how the families of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, if I have understood the story correctly, sir, they made their way down towards the shelters, closer to where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I'm -- just to be sure I have the version correct, did Mr. Mirjan and Mr. Zoran Kupreskic actually accompany their families to those places? They went with them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They passed by me, and they went on. I didn't go with them so that I knew that they went all the way. But I know that later on, they came back together, and they walked -- came past us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how long it was between the time that you saw them with their families and the time they came back? Do you know how long that was?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that about 10 to 15 minutes passed. There's about half a kilometre to my house, in one direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And if I'm again getting my time correct, and please correct me if I'm wrong, was it during the period that they were away from you that you saw these 30-odd armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll ask you: Was it daylight at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was early in the morning and it was still twilight. It had not dawned completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that some things cannot be asked. He is saying that -- he is saying that it is the twilight. He is not making a distinction between the morning twilight and the dawn, the break of dawn. I think the witness should not be confused here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I don't think the question was confusing or misleading. It's just a question of asking the witness to clarify the matter. Mr. Blaxill, can you ask a question so that the witness may clarify this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From your last response, Mr. Vidovic, you appeared to indicate that it was not full daylight. Was it light enough for you to see clearly at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could see clearly, but the darkness was receding and the dawn was approaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't know if I can elicit an any more clear response on that, Your Honours. It's not going to cause, I think, a problem for identification or anything, far from it. Mr. Vidovic, you say you saw on these people that they were wearing white belts and you could obviously see police insignia. You say you saw military police insignia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And would that be HVO military police whom you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: These people then went out of your sight and disappeared, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you see any of that unit again that day?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Some time later -- I do apologise. Some little time later you say that Mr. Zoran Kupreskic and Mirjan Kupreskic returned and joined up with you, is that right, at that spot?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you all, in fact, together with Dragan Vidovic, Dragan Samija and, I think, Mirko Santic-- Sacic I'm sorry, go towards the same direction as that group of people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I thought at one point you said you followed the group. Was I mistaken in noting that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you were right. That's what he said. I have a note that he followed the unit. Those were the words that were used. Whether he meant they went in the same direction, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will clarify, Your Honour. It's appropriate to do so. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. Did you and your companions, at that point, go in the same direction that had been taken by those soldiers, those military policemen?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't. I stayed at Niko Sakic's house in the valley, the depression, and with the soldiers it was Mirko Sakic who went off and Dragan Vidovic, Grgic, Zoran, and Mirjan and Mirko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you stayed in the depression?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I stayed on that part of the road near Niko's house, on the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not long. I didn't stay at that part long. Several minutes waiting for two others to get ready, and then we went up to Bijela Zemlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give me a time of day for when you did that, when you went there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Ahmici there was shooting going on already. In the lower parts of the village it could be heard, and near the Kupreskic houses as well. Zoran came with the Didaks, and I saw them from the road and they passed by us, and we went up there. I can't tell you what time it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think we've perhaps jumped back in time. I got the impression that when you saw that group of armed military policemen, that was after you had encountered the Kupreskics for the first time near Sakic's house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And then later Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic returned and joined you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At this time you were then, I believe, in the vicinity of the house, I think you said, of Mr. Niko Vidovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic. I'm sorry. But were you not after that then guarding -- sorry. You then went to the other location to guard the shelter of Mr. Niko Vidovic. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because -- and I can show you on the map. The place where I was at is somewhere between the two shelters, towards Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that location?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for the first day, the second day and a part of the third day, and afterwards, in the afternoon hours, we went out to Pirici, Barin Gaj, up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you're saying that you remained, in fact, in that location. Did you -- for the whole of the 16th of April? Let's just deal with the 16th for now.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would go, from time to time, to them down in the depression, because the natural path towards the entrance to the mine leads right towards the Kupreskic house in the valley, in the depression. So on two or three occasions I went to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you were in a position of standing guard away from but near to the depression in the ground; is that right? You were somewhere close to it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How many companions did you have with you when you were in that position?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you the names. There was Miro Pudza, there was Mirko Grgic, Pero Jelic, Anto Brnada and Samija Miro, who afterwards went down to his own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you and that group basically stayed there the whole day in that position with other people down in the depression?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you remember at what time it was that those people went into the depression, leaving you up at the top? Was this at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The people stayed. The ones I enumerated stayed with me. They didn't go down to the depression. There was another group down there. It was Sakic, and Kupreskic and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that to be the case. The -- there was another group of people who were down in the depression. That is correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You were saying that Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic was amongst that group. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The group that was in the depression, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And was Mr. Zoran Kupreskic in the group who remained in the depression?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you say that from time to time you yourself went down there to check up on the people, to see how they were.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to exchange a few words because we had no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many times in the course of that morning, let us say before the hour of noon, you went down into the depression to speak to the people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think I went twice in the course of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give me any indication of the times at which you may have done so?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first time it was about 8.30, and the second time a little before 12.00, between 11.00 and 12.00. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: During the course of the afternoon, after the hour of 12.00, how many times did you go down into the depression?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only once, before dusk fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give us any indication at what time of day dusk fell at that time of year?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 7.00. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So over the course of the day you say that you made three visits to the depression.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think you've given a description to the Chamber that it was a very well-protected feature, had a lot of trees and vegetation around it so you couldn't see down into it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Likewise, therefore, people inside it would not necessarily be in sight of you if you were around it on guard with a group of people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So for the majority of the day you and the Kupreskics would not have been physically able to see each other?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. From one place and the other place, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you say that the shooting went on basically for the rest of that day in and around Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You had already heard that there was shooting in the vicinity of the Kupreskic houses, there had been?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And that there was obviously shooting from other directions as well?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If we try to estimate some time without being too speculative, your group of people was in that location near the depression from fairly early hours of the morning. Would you say from before 6.00? Would you think that is fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 6.00. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Presumably, if I understand you correctly, that would place, you say, Mr. Zoran Kupreskic and Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic in that depression somewhere around 6.00, in the early hours of the morning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 6.00. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I interpret correctly what you have been saying to us, the nature of that terrain was such that you could not see them and they could not see you. So if I suggest to you a possibility, you can give me an answer if you will, sir. Someone could have left that depression for a period of time, you would not have seen them and not have known that they were absent from that depression during that period; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, but had they left the depression going towards my house using the road, then I could have seen them up from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Saying they had left the depression and gone in the direction of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic's or Mr. Zoran Kupreskic's home, could someone have left the depression and gone in that direction without being observed by you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: One thing I would like to ask you, sir, is what, in fact, had happened with respect to your own family, because initially you say you left the house and left them at your home. So what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My family remained, throughout the war, in my house. They never moved from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
