utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I didn't mean for the duration of war, I mean on that day. Did your family seek shelter? Did you take them to a shelter?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed in my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So throughout the events of the 16th of April, in fact, your family just stayed in your own home?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My house is located right next to Jozo Vrbac's shelter. It's about ten metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So from that I'm presuming, so you can correct me if wrong, that you felt there was a shelter close by if an emergency arose?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did your family, in fact, seek any shelter there during the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. They stayed in my family house together with Zoran's family and Didak's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Therefore, sir, if I can put it to you: Did you consider, therefore, that the events of that day, whatever they were, your family, in that location, was safe enough from any harm?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We were not safe even in the centre of Vitez, let alone in my family house, but the house is firmly built, it has two floors, it has two concrete -- reinforced concrete plates, and in the -- it was looking onto the main road, and so that I feel that apart from the fact if the Muslims, for example, stormed the village, unless they took the family out of the house then they did not have any great need to go to a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So what you're saying, if -- I'm just trying to get the full picture here. You say, obviously, if the Muslims stormed the village, they could be taken prisoner or something and may be safer in a shelter. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Even -- the same thing -- it would have been the same had they been in the shelter just as if they were in my house. So my house was built firmly and was safe from shelling just as the shelter was. It was just as safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But did your house have any kind of underground cellar, underground basement as these other properties appeared to have had as their safety shelters?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So isn't it true to say, sir, that you, Mr. Vidovic, did not fear that your family was in sufficient danger on the 16th of April to warrant them seeking shelter in an underground shelter like many other Croat families?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My house, at the time, was 500 metres from the fighting, and I didn't think it was necessary for them to have to go into a house which was on the other side and crowded with all the other inhabitants. My wife decided to stay at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Isn't it true it's because the very nature of that action in Ahmici that day posed, in fact, no danger to your family in the Croat area of the town -- or the village, I'm sorry, and bearing in mind the target of the attacking troops? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your family was located in a Croat area in the -- in the town, predominantly, and you knew, did you not, that the nature of the attack in Ahmici that morning posed no immediate danger to your home and your family?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I went from my house I didn't know what was going to happen in Ahmici, so I couldn't foresee. I couldn't tell my wife what to do. My wife decided on her own to stay in the house. She decided to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yet the -- you had obviously had a warning of trouble because you were woken at 4.00, and it was clear that sometime after 5.00 the shooting had started, there were explosions. Did you not, at that point, even think to get home and reassess the situation, or did you still feel confident that they were in no great danger?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went home for the first time at about 7.30, and they were still in the house, and they stayed there. They didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like a moment to confer if I may, please, Your Honours. I was just thinking at this particular point, Your Honours, and noting the time, that it would be perhaps a natural break point to stop. I don't think I will be keeping this witness a very long time tomorrow morning, or Your Honours, with my cross-examination. I think it would be a little premature for me to cease and conclude it immediately today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
